[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: everyday 'switch' means flip to one setting, and 'case' reads like 'in case of X do Y', a self-contained rule. Novices therefore expect only the matching case to run. In a Java switch statement, the case labels are only entry points: execution starts at the matching label and falls through the following cases until a break.
[1] misconception (M) -> SwitchNoFallThrough: wrong rule: After the matching case runs, the switch ends even without break. Right rule: Without break, all the statements after the matching label run, including those under later case labels, until a break or the end of the switch.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> SwitchNoFallThrough: Applies the LT rule unevenly: on a trace the selector is matched correctly but execution stops at the next case label on some runs and falls through on others, or default is run even though a case matched. (here mixing in: "After the matching case runs, the switch ends even without break")

[0] names_the_element (N): Selection statement: `switch (expr) { case v1: ...; break; ... default: ... }` chooses among many alternatives by the value of one expression.
[1] states_the_rule (S): The selector is an int-like (char, byte, short, int), String or enum expression. Case labels are distinct constants of that type, and default is optional. Control jumps to the matching label (or to default, or past the switch), and the case statements usually end with break. Without a break, execution falls through into the statements of the next case; default runs when no case matches.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Order: evaluate the selector once; compare it with the case constants; jump to the matching label (else default, else skip the switch). Then execute the statements from there in order, through later labels, until a break or the closing brace.
[1] output_prediction (OP): A switch statement has no value. Its result is the effect of the case(s) run: with `day = 3`, the S&W day switch prints Wed. Without breaks, day = 5 would print Fri, then Sat.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One execution evaluates the selector once (any side effect in it happens once) and runs the statements of one entry point and any cases it falls into. It changes only what those statements change.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): A switch replaces an if-else chain only when every test is `expr == constant` on the same expression. Range tests such as the income-bracket chain (`income < 47450`) must stay an if-else chain.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Each case is normally ended by break, which exits the switch body. Leaving it out makes that case fall into the next. Inside a loop, that break exits the switch, not the loop.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: multiway dispatch or lookup. It maps one discrete value (day number, menu choice, character) to one of several actions or results. Grouped labels (`case "apple": case "banana":`) map several values to one action.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> SwitchNoFallThrough: When every case ends with break, reordering the cases does not change behaviour (labels are distinct constants). Removing one break changes behaviour for that value only. Adding a default changes only values with no matching label.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use switch for more than two mutually exclusive alternatives decided by equality of one int, char, String or enum value. Use an if-else chain for ranges, doubles or unrelated conditions. Use an array lookup (S&W 1.4) when each case only selects a value.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Without break, execution falls through into the following cases. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Any selector value whose case lacks a break: the following cases' statements also run (e.g. both Fri and Sat printed).
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Values that match no case do nothing unless a default is present. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: An out-of-range selector (day = 7) with no default: nothing happens, and a variable assigned only in the cases may stay unassigned.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Case labels must be distinct compile-time constants of the selector type, and the selector may not be double, float, long or boolean. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Duplicate `case 1:` labels, a variable as a label, or `switch (x)` with x a double.
[5] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A String selector is dereferenced. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: Switching on a String variable that is null throws NullPointerException.
wrong: After the matching case runs, the switch ends even without break. | right: Without break, statements in switch blocks fall through into the following cases.

When there are more than two mutually exclusive alternatives, a chain of if-else statements works, but a switch statement provides a direct solution that evaluates one expression against many possible values.

Both pick one of several alternatives. A switch compares one value with constant case labels and falls through without break; an else-if chain tests each condition in turn and runs only the first true branch.
Each case of a switch normally ends with break, which exits the switch body.
switch directs the flow of control to one of several case labels, depending on the value of one expression.
